issues.subcategory: Abstract may overstate absence of causal understanding
issues.description: Abstract may overstate absence of causal understanding: The abstract's phrase 'in the absence of explicit causal understanding' appears stronger than the evidence later supports. The results show that performance improved without increasing, accurate multidimensional causal models, but the paper also reports partial causal discrimination, better-than-chance understanding on some questions, and appropriate intuitions guiding exploration.
issues.quote: Here, we show that a physical artifact becomes progressively optimized across generations of social learners in the absence of explicit causal understanding. Moreover, we find that the transmission of causal models across generations has no noticeable effect on the pace of cultural evolution. The reason is that participants do not spontaneously create multidimensional causal theories but instead mainly produce simplistic models related to a salient dimension.

issues.subcategory: Overgeneralization from 2D task to complex tech
issues.description: Overgeneralization from 2D task to complex tech: The abstract's conclusion may overgeneralize from the wheel task to 'complex technologies.' The experiment is low-dimensional in the causal variables identified by the paper, and the discussion notes that compensation between dimensions may not hold for many-dimensional problems. The results support cumulative improvement in this simplified physical system without accurate multidimensional causal understanding, but they do not by themselves establish that the same process scales to the high-dimensional technologies used to motivate the paper.
issues.quote: Finally, we show that the transmission of these inaccurate theories constrains learners' exploration and has downstream effects on their understanding. These results indicate that complex technologies need not result from enhanced causal reasoning but instead can emerge from the accumulation of improvements made across generations.

issues.subcategory: Conflation of initial acceleration and initial CM height
issues.description: Conflation of initial acceleration and initial CM height: The Figure 1 caption may blur two distinct mechanical effects. Initial torque depends on the centre of mass having horizontal leverage relative to the rotation axis, whereas a higher initial centre of mass affects the potential energy available over the descent. The Methods later distinguishes these points, so the caption should avoid implying that vertical height by itself gives better initial acceleration.
issues.quote: C-D) Asymmetrical wheels do not have their centre of mass on the axis of rotation, which can give wheels better initial acceleration. Wheel C covers the distance faster than wheel D due to the higher initial position of its centre of mass.

issues.subcategory: Incorrect formula for wheel speed in m/h
issues.description: Incorrect formula for wheel speed in m/h: The speed calculation is underspecified: if descent time was recorded in seconds, $1\,\mathrm{m}/$descent time gives $\mathrm{m/s}$, whereas the reported values are in $\mathrm{m/h}$. The analysis likely used an implicit conversion, or descent time expressed in hours, but the text should make the unit conversion explicit.
issues.quote: The average wheel speed (calculated as $1 \mathrm{~m} /$ descent time) increased across generations (Generation $95 \%$ Confidence Intervals: (1.58, 9.02), mean $=5.37 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{h}$, Figure 2.A)

issues.description: Inconsistency regarding preregistration of Hypothesis 3: There seems to be an issue with the preregistration status of hypothesis 3: the text labels the prediction that inherited theories constrain exploration as preregistered, but the exploration results are later introduced as exploratory, and the Methods only identify preregistered analyses for wheel speed and understanding. The paper should distinguish the preregistered prediction from any non-preregistered operationalization or analysis of exploration behavior.
issues.quote: Inheriting a theory can also constrain participants' exploration behavior (preregistered hypothesis 3 ). For example, cognitive scientists have shown that children who are told the function of a toy engage in more limited exploration and are less likely to discover alternative functions than children ignorant of the toy's function 16, see also 17.

issues.subcategory: Dismissal of significant interaction for understanding
issues.description: Dismissal of significant interaction for understanding: The conclusion seems too broad for the reported understanding model. While the main treatment interval includes zero, the Generation $\times$ Treatment interval for understanding, $(0.03,0.81)$, is entirely positive and excludes zero, indicating a modest treatment-related difference in the generational trajectory of understanding. Thus, the Theory treatment appears to have a more positive trajectory of understanding across generations, even if the effect is small and wheel optimization was unaffected. The text should distinguish the lack of support for improved optimization from the positive interaction for understanding, as stating that these analyses do not provide substantial support for an effect on individual understanding may understate the evidence for a small interaction.
issues.quote:
participants' understanding again barely changed across generations, although participants in the very last generation had a slightly better understanding when they had inherited a theory (Treatment $95 \% \mathrm{Cl}:(-2.54,0.31)$, mean $=-1.14$; Generation $\times$ Treatment $95 \% \mathrm{Cl}:(0.03,0.81)$, mean $=0.44$, Figure 2.B). Thus, these analyses do not provide substantial support for the idea that the transmission of explicit causal
theories affects wheel optimization and individual understanding.

issues.subcategory: Null effect conclusion based on wide confidence intervals
issues.description: Null effect conclusion based on wide confidence intervals: The conclusion that transmitting explicit theories “did not help participants produce more efficient wheels” seems stronger than the reported uncertainty warrants. The Treatment and Generation × Treatment credible intervals are wide enough to include effects that could be meaningful relative to the observed generational improvement, so the result is better characterized as limited evidence for a performance benefit rather than clear evidence of no benefit.
issues.quote: As a consequence, the transmission of explicit theories across generations did not help participants produce more efficient wheels: inheriting a theory mostly constrained participants' exploration, and prevented them from noticing the effects of relevant variables outside of the theory they received.

issues.subcategory: Confounding intuitions with in-task learning and transmission
issues.description: Confounding intuitions with in-task learning and transmission: The attribution of non-random exploration to participants’ “appropriate intuitions” may need qualification unless the pattern is shown before feedback and cultural transmission could operate. If the observation is based on configurations pooled across trials or generations, within-participant learning and inherited configurations could also explain why centres of mass clustered in relatively useful regions.
issues.quote: It is worth noting that despite exhibiting poor understanding of the experimental physical system, participants did not randomly explore the parameter space. For example, in both treatments, wheels were much more likely to have their centre of mass at the center of the wheel, or in the upper right quadrant. This indicates that participants had appropriate intuitions about how to maximize acceleration, and sampled the parameter space fairly efficiently in that regard.

issues.subcategory: Conflation of torque, angular momentum, and inertia
issues.description: Conflation of torque, angular momentum, and inertia: The mechanical explanation conflates angular momentum with angular velocity. By definition, net torque is the rate of change of angular momentum. Therefore, a smaller moment of inertia does not decrease the torque needed to change angular momentum. Instead, a smaller moment of inertia yields a greater angular acceleration for a given torque, allowing the wheel to reach a higher angular velocity in the same time. The text must describe this fundamental physical mechanism accurately.
issues.quote: Wheels with a smaller moment of inertia (i.e. wheels that have their weights closer to the axis) require less torque to increase angular momentum and spin faster

issues.subcategory: The assumed acceleration-inertia tradeoff has a counterexample
issues.description: The assumed acceleration-inertia tradeoff has a counterexample: This tradeoff holds when shifting top or side weights outward, but it is not universally true. If a participant moves the bottom weight radially inward, the vertical center of mass moves upward (improving initial acceleration), while the overall contribution to moment of inertia simultaneously decreases. Generalized claims about a strict physical tradeoff between these two parameters mischaracterize the actual design space participants explored. Clarify that this tradeoff applies only to specific directional weight manipulations.
issues.quote: A higher centre of mass can produce better acceleration but it will increasethe wheel's moment of inertia and so there was a tradeoff between maximizing acceleration and minimizing inertia

issues.subcategory: Central weight plates cannot reduce absolute inertia
issues.description: Central weight plates cannot reduce absolute inertia: Adding mass anywhere on a physical object strictly increases its absolute moment of inertia. Adding 1 kg of central ballast cannot shrink the wheel's intrinsic moment of inertia. The authors likely mean this ballast reduces the specific moment of inertia (inertia divided by total mass) compared to a design lacking central mass, diminishing the relative penalty of the exterior weights. Rewrite this description so it does not imply a violation of basic mass superposition.
issues.quote: Two 500 -gram weight plates were positioned along the axis of the wheel (one on each side of the clamp) in order to reduce the wheel's moment of inertia

issues.subcategory: Missing scoring rule for tied performance judgments
issues.description: Missing scoring rule for tied performance judgments: The testing phase explicitly includes a third answer option for perceived equivalence. The manuscript never explains when, or if, this response was evaluated as correct. If every forced-choice pair contained a mathematically faster configuration, then "No difference" was predictably always marked incorrect. State the exact grading rule for this tertiary option so the theoretical maximum score is unambiguous.
issues.quote: For each pair, participants could submit 3 possible answers: "Wheel 1", "Wheel 2" or "No difference".

issues.subcategory: Payoff formula in Participants' payoff may allow negative rewards
issues.description: Payoff formula in Participants' payoff may allow negative rewards: The payoff formula as written appears to yield negative per-wheel payoffs whenever RecordedSpeed is below MinSpeed, and the handling of non-descending wheels is not specified here. This is difficult to reconcile with the stated additional payment range of 0 to 26 € unless payoffs were floored at zero, failures were handled outside this formula, or RecordedSpeed was otherwise constrained.
issues.quote:
## Participants' payoff

The following equation determined the payoff of each wheel:
[1 - ((MaxSpeed - RecordedSpeed) / (MaxSpeed - MinSpeed)) ] x $3+$ Bonus
with MaxSpeed $=160$, MinSpeed $=96$. RecordedSpeed was the recorded average speed of the wheel. Bonus took the value 0.2 for wheels that descended and 0 otherwise.

Participants' final payoff corresponded to the sum of the payoff of each of their wheels plus the payoff of the next participant' first two wheels plus $5 €$ if they correctly answered the randomly selected test. Final participants in chains had their last two payoffs doubled

issues.subcategory: Incongruent reliability statistic for five raters
issues.description: Incongruent reliability statistic for five raters: The previous sentence states that five individuals coded the theories. Standard Cohen's kappa is defined strictly for two raters. Readers cannot deduce how this single statistic was derived from a five-rater pool. State explicitly whether this value represents Fleiss' kappa, an unweighted arithmetic mean of ten pairwise Cohen's kappas, or agreement computed against a master consensus code.
issues.quote: Cohen's kappa coefficients reveal almost perfect agreement between raters ( 0.81 for inertia and 0.85 for centre of mass).

issues.subcategory: Missing coding schemes for linear model parameters
issues.description: Missing coding schemes for linear model parameters: The interpretation of the reported interaction terms depends heavily on how the variables are coded. If Generation is treated as a continuous arithmetic sequence (1 through 5), the interaction tests for divergent linear slopes. If Generation is a five-level categorical factor, the interaction estimates generation-specific contrasts. Specify the exact coding scheme utilized for Trial and Generation in the methods, as this dictates the functional meaning of the parameter estimates.
issues.quote: We fitted a linear model with "Speed" as the outcome variable, "Trial", "Generation", "Treatment", "Trial:Treatment" and "Generation:Treatment" as predictor variables

issues.subcategory: Deviation rationale for Analysis 4 is hard to follow
issues.description: Deviation rationale for Analysis 4 is hard to follow: The rationale for deviating from the preregistered Analysis 4 is not fully clear. The negative correlation between inertia and centre-of-mass scores is itself substantively important, so it is not obvious why that pattern required aggregating across physical principles or why it caused the preregistered principle-specific model not to converge.
issues.quote:
## Deviation from preregistered analyses

In preregistered analysis 4, the outcome variable was "Score" and each participant was associated with 2 values in the dataset: one score for inertia, the other for centre of mass. As compared to the analysis we ran, the preregistered model included "Physical Principle" and "Physical Principle: Treatment" as predictor variables and "Player's identity" as random effect. However, analyses revealed that understanding scores about inertia and centre of mass were negatively correlated (Supplementary Figure 9 and Supplementary Table 7) and some individuals better understood inertia than centre of mass while others better understood centre of mass than inertia (Figure 3I and Supplementary Figure 2). As a result, the preregistered model did not converge so we ran our analysis on aggregated score and removed the terms associated the variable "Physical Principle" in the reported model.

issues.description: Aggregated score obscures unidimensional understanding: Aggregating inertia and centre-of-mass scores is potentially misleading for claims about unchanged understanding unless the interpretation is explicitly limited to overall multidimensional accuracy. Given the reported negative correlation and skewed principle-specific profiles, the aggregate score can miss changes in which principle participants understand, even if total test performance remains flat.
issues.quote: However, analyses revealed that understanding scores about inertia and centre of mass were negatively correlated (Supplementary Figure 9 and Supplementary Table 7) and some individuals better understood inertia than centre of mass while others better understood centre of mass than inertia (Figure 3I and Supplementary Figure 2). As a result, the preregistered model did not converge so we ran our analysis on aggregated score and removed the terms associated the variable "Physical Principle" in the reported model.

{"overall": "**Construct validity of causal understanding**

The manuscript frames its central finding around the idea that causal understanding is not necessary for technological improvement, as seen in the title and abstract. However, the exact measures—the 10-item prediction test and the written theories in the "Configurations + Theory" treatment—specifically evaluate explicit, verbalizable, post-task causal knowledge.

The paper notes that participants "did not randomly explore the parameter space" and possessed "appropriate intuitions" that successfully biased them toward useful center-of-mass regions. These implicit physical intuitions, analogies, or payoff-guided heuristics constitute a form of causal cognition. Restricting the cognitive-versus-cultural niche contrast to explicit multidimensional theories, rather than broadly rejecting causal understanding, will align the theoretical claims directly with what the experimental design tests.


**Decomposing generation-level improvements**

The generation effect in the "Configurations" treatment establishes that later generations produce faster final wheels. By itself, this trend leaves open the possibility that the improvement reflects repeated individual convergence from increasingly advantageous starting points, rather than "the accumulation of many improvements made across generations" via selective retention.

Each participant is given their predecessor’s last two configurations, then completes five independent trials in a low-dimensional design space featuring highly salient affordances. Unpacking the existing trial-level chain data to detail inherited performance, within-participant improvements, and the rates at which variant configurations are rejected or retained across lineages would clarify whether cumulative cultural selection is the primary operational mechanism driving the aggregate trend.


**Aggregation in the prediction test**

The conclusion that understanding does not increase rests on a 10-item post-task test, comprising five moment-of-inertia items, five center-of-mass items, and a "No difference" option. The baseline chance for this task and the scoring rules for the "No difference" option require clarification in the main text to anchor the results.

Because the preregistered principle-level model failed to converge, the analyses aggregate the understanding scores. The manuscript importantly documents that inertia and center-of-mass understanding often trade off across participants. Aggregating these dimensions can mask structured, principle-specific learning, turning focused acquisition of local knowledge into an apparent absence of overall improvement. Providing item-level and principle-level estimates, alongside sensitivity checks for the scoring assumptions, will establish whether the test is reliable and sensitive enough to capture localized understanding.


**Boundary conditions of the theory transmission effect**

The conclusion that theory transmission has no noticeable effect on cultural evolution generalizes beyond what the specific manipulation tests. The generated theories represent narrow, novice-crafted statements written after the test phase, transmitted one generation at a time, and deliberately isolated from performance-specific configuration data. In the dataset, only 6 of 56 participants inherited a full theory.

Statistically, the generation-by-treatment confidence intervals for speed (Generation $\times$ Treatment $95\%$ CI: (-7.07, 2.52)) do not rule out practically meaningful effects. Reframing this contribution to emphasize the positive finding—that spontaneously generated unidimensional theories canalize design exploration and redistribute principle-specific understanding—offers a highly robust conclusion supported directly by the evidence.


**Model specifications for wheel performance**

The main speed analyses apply linear models to trial-level speed, encode non-descending wheels as having zero speed, restrict the data to the final two trials, and use participant and chain random intercepts. In contrast, Figure 2 highlights conditional speed specifically among non-failures.

Treating failure to descend as a speed of zero transforms a distinct binary outcome into an extremely slow successful run. Furthermore, trial-level observations may overstate the informativeness of the data given the lineage constraint, as cultural chains operate as the independent evolutionary units.
